As the election follows the preferential voting system, counting is expected to continue for several rounds, with the final result likely to be declared late in the evening or around midnight.The constituency, which covers Dharwad, Haveri, Gadag and Uttara Kannada districts, recorded a voter turnout of 75.6% in the October 23 election. Of the 97,400 registered voters, 73,658 cast their votes.A candidate needs to secure 50% plus one of the valid votes to win in the first round. Fourteen candidates are in the fray, including BJP’s SV Sankanur, who won the seat in 2014 and 2020, Congress candidate Mohan Limbikai and independent candidate Kanthkumar.Regional commissioner and returning officer KM Janaki said on Monday that votes would be counted across 14 tables. articles.title: Stanford economists have a warning for California on its proposed Billionaires' Tax; says it may leave the State poorer by ...
articles.summary: California's proposed billionaire tax could generate far less revenue than supporters project and may ultimately leave the state nearly $39 billion worse
articles.body: California's proposed billionaire tax could generate far less revenue than supporters project and may ultimately leave the state nearly $39 billion worse off, according to a new analysis by two economists affiliated with Stanford University's Hoover Institution. According to a report by Fortune, the warning comes as voters prepare to decide on Proposition 40 in the 3 November election. The ballot measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of California residents who were billionaires as of 1 January 2026, with supporters claiming it could raise about $100 billion for the state, around 90% of which would be directed toward healthcare spending.What Proposition 40 would doThe measure is on California’s November 3 ballot. It would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of the state’s few hundred billionaires who were residents on January 1, 2026, with payment due in 2027. Those who choose to spread payments over five years would pay more. Real estate, pensions and most retirement accounts would generally be excluded.Revenue estimate far below supporters' projectionsIn a working paper published this month by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), economists Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh estimate the measure would raise only about $30 billion, with a likely range of $28 billion to $36 billion. That is less than one-third of the revenue forecast by proponents of the tax.According to the researchers, a major reason for the lower estimate is the migration of wealthy residents out of California. The study analysed Forbes billionaire rankings, real estate records and public relocation announcements to conclude that billionaire departures have already reduced the potential tax base by nearly 30%.The economists pointed to several high-profile billionaires who have publicly moved from California, including Peter Thiel and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. Together, seven billionaires who have announced relocations account for an estimated $540 billion in wealth, according to the study.Why researchers forecast a $39 billion lossThe Stanford-affiliated economists argue that the larger issue is not the initial tax collection but the potential long-term loss of income tax revenue if wealthy residents continue leaving the state. The study estimates billionaire departures could reduce California's annual income tax collections by between $1 billion and $3.5 billion. If those losses persist indefinitely, they would outweigh the one-time wealth tax proceeds by approximately $38.9 billion in present-value terms.To test various outcomes, the researchers ran 100,000 simulations using different assumptions for revenue generation and discount rates. They found that 85% of scenarios resulted in a net financial loss for the state. The findings represent a more pessimistic outlook than an earlier analysis from the Hoover Institution, which projected roughly $40 billion in revenue and a net loss of about $25 billion.‘Billionaires can move’The economists’ main explanation is that billionaires can leave. Using Forbes rankings, real estate reports and public relocation announcements, they estimate that departures have already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the proposed tax base. CBS News, citing the study, reported that seven billionaires who have publicly moved out of California account for about $540 billion in wealth, including Peter Thiel and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The estimate also discounts the remaining base for the risk that courts strike the tax down. The new figure is a sharper downgrade than the authors’ earlier Hoover analysis, which projected about $40 billion in revenue and a $25 billion net loss.Other economists disagreeNot all economists share the Stanford researchers' conclusions. A separate study by economists Jasper Boll, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, also published through the NBER, argued that even if every billionaire permanently left California, it would take around 25 years for lost income tax collections to equal the projected $100 billion windfall from the tax. The authors also challenged the assumption that billionaire departures would have permanent effects. They argued that if California does not introduce recurring wealth taxes, some billionaires could eventually return, while newly created fortunes could replenish the state's billionaire population.Meanwhile, California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office has offered a more moderate forecast, estimating the measure could raise tens of billions of dollars over several years while reducing annual income tax revenue by less than $1 billion.Fierce political battle underwayThe proposal has triggered one of California's most expensive ballot fights. According to campaign finance disclosures cited by reports, technology billionaires have contributed more than $340 million to oppose the measure and support competing ballot initiatives. Sergey Brin alone has reportedly donated more than $100 million, while other donors include former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt, Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, Stripe chief executive Patrick Collison and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. Opponents have spent at least $21.2 million during the first 19 days of September, according to the report.California Governor Gavin Newsom has also opposed the billionaire tax, arguing it could encourage wealthy residents to leave the state along with their income tax payments. Earlier this month, Newsom endorsed Proposition 42, a competing ballot measure backed by Brin that would effectively block Proposition 40 by banning new state taxes on personal property and retroactive taxation.You use AI every day. articles.body: Former Miss Switzerland Beatrice Keul has alleged that US President Donald Trump raped her in 1993 at the Plaza Hotel in New York, describing the alleged assault as “brutal”.Her account features in a new report released by Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee examining Trump's alleged links to Jeffrey Epstein's sex trafficking operation.Keul, then a young Swiss model and financial services professional, was recruited in November 1993 by Jill Harth to attend the Donald Trump's American Dream Pageant for contestants aged 16 to 22 in Atlantic City and New York.What report saysDuring a press luncheon at the then Trump-owned Plaza Hotel, Trump approached Keul and introduced himself, saying, “Finally we meet Ms Keul”.Later that day, a representative of Trump invited Keul upstairs at the Plaza Hotel to meet the president, according to the report. Believing the meeting could help advance her career and education, she went with the representative.Keul alleged that Trump grabbed her from behind and forcibly raped her upon entering the suite, tearing her dress and leaving her bleeding and bruised. She described the assault as “brutal”.Following the alleged assault, Trump repeated his offers to arrange a visa and university admission and made her promise to remain silent, according to her account. He allegedly told her, “[T]he show must go on.”Keul said she completed the pageant in a terrified “daze”. Her passport had been taken from her on arrival, and she feared that asking for its return before the contest ended would alert Trump that something was wrong, the report said.The Epstein linkAccording to her account, Trump offered to help her obtain a US visa and secure admission to New York University (NYU), repeatedly assuring her that he would take care of her arrangements.After Trump left their conversation, Epstein approached Keul, introducing himself as “I’m Jeffrey, Don’s best friend.” He allegedly offered similar assistance and invited her to a party at Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in the coming months. “You know I can take care of you. We organize many parties with Don,” Epstein said according to Keul's account.After the assault, she returned to Switzerland and declined to participate in another Trump-sponsored pageant in Hawaii several weeks later. According to the report, Trump called her in Switzerland several months after the alleged assault and again offered to arrange a visa and admission to NYU. She declined.White House denies allegationsThe White House rejected Keul's allegations. “None of these allegations are true,” People quoted White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis as saying.Bis described the report as “nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements.”She added, “The President kicked Jeffrey Epstein out of his club at Mar-a-Lago because he was a creep, and he has been fully exonerated of anything related to Epstein.”Trump has not been charged with a crime in connection with Keul's allegations. articles.body: A US Marine has been indicted on charges of murder and robbery in connection with the death of a 39-year-old Japanese woman in Okinawa, a case that has sparked protests and renewed calls for accountability over the presence of US military personnel in Japan.Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is accused of killing Anna Yagi at a hotel in Naha, the prefectural capital, on October 3.Japanese public broadcaster NHK reported that prosecutors indicted Ballard on Sunday, alleging that he strangled Yagi with a telephone cord and stole her backpack and wallet. Ballard has denied the allegations, although Japanese media reports citing investigators said some of his statements suggested involvement in the incident.Security footage reportedly showed a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with Yagi and leaving alone with her belongings.The killing has triggered public anger, with around 100 people protesting in Naha and Tokyo earlier this month. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the incident as “brutal and heinous”, while her government lodged a strong protest with the US and called for strict disciplinary action against military personnel and measures to prevent similar incidents.Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture had repeatedly urged the US to take steps to prevent such cases, adding that the alleged crime pointed to a lack of discipline.The US Marine Corps earlier said it was cooperating with Japanese authorities over allegations of serious criminal conduct and expressed condolences to Yagi's family.The case has also prompted a curfew and an alcohol ban for US service members stationed in Okinawa.The island hosts the largest concentration of US military personnel in Japan, which has around 55,000 American troops. Their presence has long been a source of local opposition, with previous crimes involving US servicemen triggering protests.In 1995, tens of thousands of people demonstrated after three US servicemen abducted and raped a 12-year-old Japanese girl. More recently, several sexual assault cases involving US military personnel in Okinawa have fuelled demands for stronger safeguards and accountability.Takaichi said her government had urged Washington to take thorough measures to prevent a recurrence of such incidents.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Arun Chauhan, the Haryana farmer who moved away from paddy to a 75-day sweet corn crop, says he now makes nearly Rs 25 lakh a year, and helped a village build an 80-member, Rs 4-crore farming collective
articles.summary: In 2004, Arun Chauhan’s family earned around Rs 10,000 from paddy cultivation on their farmland in Manauli village in Haryana’s Sonipat district.
articles.body: In 2004, Arun Chauhan’s family earned around Rs 10,000 from paddy cultivation on their farmland in Manauli village in Haryana’s Sonipat district. Nearly two decades later, the 59-year-old farmer has shifted much of his land to sweet corn and vegetables, says he earns a profit of nearly Rs 25 lakh a year from sweet corn, and has helped build a farmers’ collective with 80 members and an annual turnover of nearly Rs 4 crore.As reported by The Indian Express, Chauhan’s decision to move away from the traditional paddy-wheat cycle came after he visited a friend’s farm where strawberries were being cultivated successfully. The change began on a portion of his family’s 28 acres. Initially, sweet corn was grown on 10 acres. That area has since increased to 17 acres, while seven acres are used for vegetables in polyhouses and net houses. Two acres are earmarked for a packhouse and another two for fisheries.A crop that takes 75 daysOne reason Chauhan favours sweet corn is its short growing period. The crop takes about 75 days, allowing him to cultivate three cycles in a year. According to The Indian Express, Chauhan said sweet corn fetches an average price of Rs 12-14 per kg throughout the year. With an average production of 50 quintals per acre, he estimates gross returns of Rs 60,000-70,000 per acre. After deducting cultivation expenses of around Rs 15,000–20,000, he puts the profit at nearly Rs 50,000 per acre.Manauli becomes a ‘sweet corn village’The shift has extended beyond Chauhan’s own farm. He told The Indian Express that nearly all of Manauli’s 2,000 acres of agricultural land had been under paddy almost two decades ago. Today, he estimates that 70% of the village’s farmland is used for sweet corn and vegetables, with sweet corn alone grown on around 800 acres.As per an earlier report by Krishi Jagran, Manauli had transitioned towards sweet corn and vegetables, including crops grown under protected cultivation. Its 2022 report said the village had become known for sweet corn and that farmers were increasingly adopting alternative crops.The village’s location also gives farmers access to a large market. Delhi’s Azadpur Mandi, one of the country’s major wholesale markets for fresh produce, is about 20 km away. Farmers are also looking beyond traditional wholesale markets. According to Chauhan, e-commerce companies have entered into direct arrangements with local farmers to buy sweet corn and fresh vegetables.Why crop diversification mattersManauli’s experience comes amid wider efforts to encourage farmers in Haryana to diversify beyond the paddy-wheat system. In a December 2025 statement, the Press Information Bureau, citing the Union Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, said Haryana had been implementing the ‘Mera Pani Meri Virasat’ scheme since 2020 to encourage farmers to move away from paddy towards alternative crops, partly in response to declining groundwater levels. The scheme is part of the broader policy context for crop diversification, although the available information does not establish that it directly supported Chauhan’s decision to grow sweet corn.For Chauhan and the farmers working with him, the change has involved more than replacing paddy with another crop. Shorter growing cycles, access to Delhi’s wholesale market, direct sales and collective processing have created additional ways to earn from their land. Manauli’s experience shows how a village’s farming choices can change when farmers organise production around what the market is willing to buy.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: After their father died in 2017, a Texas grandfather gained custody of three children and sought unpaid support from their mother; an October 23 appeals court upheld a $93,778 judgment, including $65,532 in medical costs
articles.summary: A Texas grandfather who became the primary caregiver of his three grandchildren following their father's death has won a legal battle against their mother
articles.body: A Texas grandfather who became the primary caregiver of his three grandchildren following their father's death has won a legal battle against their mother over unpaid child support and medical bills. Last week, a Texas appeals court upheld a $93,778 judgment against the mother, including more than $65,000 in medical expenses.As detailed in the court ruling available on Justia, Rain Levy Minns Udall and her husband divorced in 2016, with both retaining legal responsibility for their three children. Soon afterwards, the father was diagnosed with cancer. He died in November 2017.Four years later, the children's grandfather, Michael Minns, went to court seeking responsibility for their care. His first application concerned only the eldest child, but he later asked to take responsibility for all three. The court eventually granted him sole managing conservatorship, making him the children's primary legal caregiver.The court had also ordered Udall to contribute financially towards her children's upbringing and healthcare. When Minns claimed that these payments were not being made, he returned to court seeking the outstanding money.How payment dispute reached courtAt a hearing, the trial court examined the payments required from Udall and what she had actually paid. It found seven instances of unpaid monthly child support and seven instances of unpaid cash medical support. There were also 118 violations relating to medical expenses. The court further found that an earlier child-support judgment of $14,192.71 remained unpaid.It awarded Minns another $93,778.44. Of this amount, $65,532.40 concerned medical expenses that had not been reimbursed. The remaining sum covered $13,136.48 in unpaid child support, $643.31 in medical support and $14,467.25 in lawyers' fees.Udall appealed, arguing that the order should not stand. Her objections centred on the medical expenses and whether the grandfather had followed the required process before asking her to pay.Mother questioned medical expensesThe medical bills covered treatment received by the children between July 2021 and March 2024. The court records also noted that all three children had significant mental healthcare needs alongside physical healthcare expenses.Under the arrangements made in 2021, Udall was responsible for all healthcare expenses not covered by insurance if she was not providing the children's insurance. The later custody order continued to place responsibility for these costs on her, subject to provisions concerning the deceased father's estate. Despite those arrangements, Minns asked the court to recover only half of the outstanding medical expenses.Udall maintained that he had not given her the necessary documents on time. She also raised concerns about the choice of healthcare providers and argued that she had not been properly consulted about treatment decisions.The appeals court examined these objections but found that she had not identified particular bills that were unsupported or incorrect. It also found no requirement making prior consultation a condition for recovering the expenses.Another important question was whether late paperwork meant the mother no longer had to pay. The court explained that the orders allowed additional time for reimbursement when documents were supplied late.How grandfather supported his claimMinns had presented detailed spreadsheets showing the healthcare expenses incurred for each child. The records included the treatment dates, providers, amounts paid and the money he was seeking from Udall. They also showed when the relevant information had been sent to her and when payment was expected.During the hearing, Minns confirmed that the records reflected the expenses he had incurred and the reimbursements received. He said Udall had made only one payment towards those medical expenses.The appeals court found it significant that Udall had not disputed that the treatment expenses were incurred. Nor had she challenged individual entries in the spreadsheets or provided specific examples of inadequate supporting documents.The judges therefore concluded that the grandfather's records, together with his testimony, provided sufficient grounds for the trial court to award the outstanding medical expenses.What happened to the mother's appealThe mother had another objection. She argued that the custody proceedings should have been handled by the court that dealt with her divorce rather than a different district court in Travis County.The appeals court rejected this argument, explaining that the county's system allowed district judges to hear matters within the relevant court's jurisdiction.There was also a separate disagreement over punishment for unpaid support. The trial court had ordered two-week jail terms for certain violations, with the terms running at the same time, but had suspended imprisonment.Udall challenged that decision as well. However, the appeals court said contempt orders must be challenged through a different legal process and therefore did not decide that part of her case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 10L people, 20k vehicles, Rs 10k cr loss: Why traders' body want Rahul's Nov 1 rally postponed
articles.summary: The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) has urged Congress leader Rahul Gandhi to postpone the party’s proposed November 1 rally at Delhi’s Ramlila
articles.body: The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) has urged Congress leader Rahul Gandhi to postpone the party’s proposed November 1 rally at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan, warning that it could disrupt business across 21 major wholesale and retail markets during the peak festive shopping season and cause losses of up to Rs 10,000 crore.The traders’ body has asked Congress to defer the rally until November 10, after Bhai Dooj, or shift it to an alternative venue away from commercial areas. The Congress has claimed that the rally could draw 10 lakh people.In a letter to Rahul Gandhi, a copy of which was also sent to Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, CTI chairman Brijesh Goyal raised concerns about possible barricading and road closures on October 31 and November 1. He said traders were worried about whether customers would be able to reach shops during the crucial festive period, news agency PTI reported.10 lakh people, up to 20,000 vehiclesAccording to the CTI, a gathering of 10 lakh people could bring between 15,000 and 20,000 vehicles into Delhi. These could include 10,000 to 12,000 buses and 5,000 to 7,000 smaller vehicles, such as cars, minibuses and tempo travellers.The organisation questioned where these vehicles would be parked, claiming there was no authorised parking facility for even 200 vehicles in the immediate vicinity of Ramlila Maidan.It also warned that congestion could spill into the narrow lanes of Old Delhi, many of which are only 10 to 12 feet wide. A single truck getting stuck in these lanes could trigger traffic jams lasting several hours, it said.21 markets at riskThe CTI identified 21 markets that could be affected by the rally, including Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar, Khari Baoli, Bhagirath Palace, Chawri Bazaar, Kashmere Gate, Karol Bagh, Daryaganj, Paharganj, Jama Masjid and Lajpat Rai Market.The body cited the October 10 event at Jantar Mantar, claiming that a gathering of around 3,000 to 4,000 people had disrupted movement across central Delhi and caused traders losses of Rs 3,000 crore.It projected that the November 1 rally could bring commercial activity across Old Delhi to a standstill, with losses potentially reaching Rs 10,000 crore.The CTI has proposed Burari Ground or Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium as alternative venues if the rally cannot be postponed. It has urged the Congress leadership to consider the concerns of traders and minimise disruption to business during the festive season.'We hear you': Rahul GandhiCongress leader Rahul Gandhi expressed solidarity with Delhi’s traders, alleging that government restrictions had disrupted business by shutting metro services, sealing roads and locking down the capital.Linking the disruption to his allegations of “vote chori”, Rahul demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi sack Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, whom he referred to as “Accused No. 4”.“To every trader in Delhi: We love you and hear you. The Govt shut the metro, sealed our roads and locked down our capital. With a stolen vote nothing is safe - your shop, your savings, your children’s future. Tell Modi to sack accused no. 4, Gyanesh Kumar and the protests will stop in 30 seconds,” Rahul said.Traders reported losses after Oct 10 protestDelhi traders sought Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s intervention over losses allegedly caused by the October 10 protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), demanding compensation from those responsible for the disruption.The Automotive Parts Merchants Association (Regd.), Delhi, said customers stayed away from markets for four to five days before and after the protest call, resulting in heavy business losses.The association had said October, November and December were crucial for traders because of the festive season, including Navratri, Dhanteras and Diwali. It warned that repeated disruptions during this period could threaten the livelihoods of shopkeepers and their employees.The trade body called for a transparent assessment of the losses and sought full compensation from the principal organisers and participants responsible for the disruption, arguing that traders should not bear the financial burden.It said shop earnings were used to support traders’ families and employees, pay rent, fund children’s education and cover medical expenses for elderly parents.The association also flagged the absence of basic emergency arrangements, including ambulances, fire services and first aid, at protests, warning that such gaps could lead to serious accidents.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A data centre built beside homes in Wales has sparked protests over noise, traffic and property values as the UK expands its AI infrastructure
articles.summary: A data centre built beside homes in Newport, South Wales, has raised concerns among residents about construction noise, traffic, its visual impact and
articles.body: A data centre built beside homes in Newport, South Wales, has raised concerns among residents about construction noise, traffic, its visual impact and potential effects on property prices. According to BBC Wales, the Vantage Data Centre Campus is planned to include three data centres across 46 acres. Residents have questioned how the development could affect their neighbourhood, while the company says it works with local authorities to manage construction activity. Similar concerns have emerged over a proposed data centre in Cardiff, bringing wider questions about the environmental impact, resource demands and planning of Britain’s expanding data centre sector.How is the data centre affecting nearby residentsAnother resident, Anthony, who lives near Amanda, also raised concerns about the effect of the development on the surrounding neighbourhood. He said the construction work was affecting the area's previous tranquillity because of noise and additional traffic. Anthony described the impact by saying that the construction “takes away the peace from the neighbourhood”. His comments reflected concerns about the disruption associated with building a large data centre close to existing homes.Vantage Data Centre responded by stating that it was “committed to being a good neighbour”. A spokesperson for the company said it worked closely with local authorities to manage construction activity, including traffic, noise and lighting. The company also said it incorporated measures designed to protect the local environment. Newport City Council said that, when considering planning applications, it worked to “ensure that the impacts are considered acceptable in terms of biodiversity, light, noise and construction traffic”. The statements set out the company's and council's approaches to managing the potential effects of the development.Why are Cardiff residents opposing the proposed data centreConcerns about the effects of data centres on nearby communities have also emerged in Cardiff, where campaigners are opposing proposals for a data centre campus at Llanrumney. The proposed development would occupy the site of Cardiff East Park & Ride, which provides transport for passengers travelling to the University Hospital of Wales. Sue Elias, who uses the service and has campaigned against the proposal alongside the residents' union Acorn, said she understood the need for data centres but believed there should be a pause to consider where they were built. “They shouldn't just be put up and then worry about the consequences afterwards,” she said.The Cardiff and Vale University Health Board described the park and ride as an “essential transport link” and said it was “committed to identifying a suitable and convenient alternative location”. Local campaigners have also raised concerns about the potential environmental effects of the proposed development. Lizzie Bailey, who lives locally, described the planned data centre as “an environmental nightmare both for the wildlife and the local residents”. She also warned about possible disruption from construction and the subsequent operation of diesel generators and cooling fans. However, Curtis Hall Ltd, the company behind the plans, said the development would “not put a strain on the energy grid or water infrastructure”. The company also said a detailed noise impact assessment had concluded that the site would not have an adverse noise impact on the nearest homes, including at night.Why is the UK seeing a rise in data centresThe concerns in Newport and Cardiff come as the number of data centres across the UK increases in response to growing demand for computing capacity, including for artificial intelligence. The BBC report stated that 568 data centres were listed in the UK, according to the Data Centre Map, and cited research suggesting that the number could increase by almost a fifth, with nine proposed in Wales. Data centres support digital services such as online banking and movie streaming, while the UK government classifies them as critical national infrastructure. Their expansion has nevertheless raised questions about electricity demand, grid capacity, water consumption, land use, biodiversity and the effects on communities near proposed sites.Figures cited in the BBC report illustrate the scale of the resource requirements. Ofgem said the electricity capacity requested by data centre projects seeking to connect to the grid had increased from 41GW to 125GW in the preceding year. Water UK estimated that data centres used approximately 6.6 million litres of water a day, equivalent to the amount used by 20,000 average homes. Senedd Research identified potential benefits, including jobs, investment, skills development and support for innovation, while also highlighting significant resource and policy questions. Professor Alan Brown of the University of Exeter, author of Making AI Work for Britain, said authorities should be “a lot more engaged” with communities when data centres were being developed. He warned that if community involvement was bypassed, residents could feel they were “getting all of the pain and none of the benefit”.Why are campaigners calling for stricter data centre rulesThe debate has also prompted calls for stronger controls over new developments. Friends of the Earth has called for a UK-wide pause on new data centres until clear rules are established on their energy and water use. Kierra Box, from the organisation, said the group wanted safeguards to ensure data centres did not consume resources needed elsewhere. The UK government, meanwhile, said planning applications were required to consider the effects on communities and the environment, and pointed to plans to support development through increased clean power capacity and AI Growth Zones. The Welsh government said new developments remained subject to the planning system and environmental regulation. While the potential effect of the Newport development on local property values remains a concern raised by residents, the BBC report did not establish that house prices had fallen as a result. It also reported concerns about visual impact and light, but did not establish that the data centre had blocked sunlight to neighbouring homes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Student gets admission elsewhere and withdraws from IIHMCA before classes begin, but institute cites 'non refundable' fee clause and refuses refund; Hyderabad consumer commission orders Rs 39,500 in relief
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A consumer commission in Telangana has held the Indian Institute of Hotel Management and Culinary Arts (IIHMCA) guilty for refusing to refund a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A consumer commission in Telangana has held the Indian Institute of Hotel Management and Culinary Arts (IIHMCA) guilty for refusing to refund a student's admission fee after he withdrew before the academic session began.The commission directed the institute to refund Rs 29,500 after deducting Rs 1,000 as processing charges, besides paying Rs 5,000 as compensation and Rs 5,000 towards litigation expenses.Student withdrew admission after securing a seat elsewhereAccording to the commission order, Nikhil Sai, an 18-year-old student, had been provisionally admitted to IIHMCA in Hyderabad in May 2025. His mother, M Bhargavi, an advocate, represented him in the consumer complaint.The student paid Rs 30,500 towards the provisional admission fee on May 3, 2025. The amount included Rs 500 towards the application fee and Rs 9,000 and Rs 21,000 towards provisional admission, the order said.The complainant said the institute had assured them that the fee would be refunded if the student withdrew before classes began. Subsequently, he secured admission to another institution under the National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology (NCHMCT).His mother sought withdrawal and a refund on July 1, 2025, before the commencement of the academic session. However, the institute refused to return the fee, citing a condition printed on the receipts stating that the amount was non-refundable.The complainant approached the commission seeking a refund of Rs 29,500 after deducting Rs 1,000 as processing charges. She also sought 12% annual interest on the amount, Rs 50,000 as compensation for mental agony and harassment, and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.The commission noted that the institute did not appear despite service of notice and was proceeded against ex parte. The complainant's evidence and documents, including payment receipts, email correspondence and WhatsApp messages, remained unchallenged.Why did the commission hold the institute liable?The bench comprising president Chitneni Latha Kumari and members D Madhavi Latha and Kathyayani Khandavilli examined the payment receipts, the student's withdrawal request and the applicable University Grants Commission (UGC) fee-refund guidelines.The commission noted that the student had sought withdrawal before the academic session began and had not attended any classes or received study material or other educational services from the institute.It said the institution could not justify retaining the entire fee merely by relying on a printed non-refundable condition when the admission was provisional and withdrawal was sought before classes began.“The material placed on record, including the UGC refund guidelines forming part of Ex.A2, supports the Complainant's contention that where withdrawal takes place before commencement of the academic session, the institution cannot retain the entire fee merely by relying upon a general non-refundable clause,” the commission said.The commission referred to the UGC's fee-refund guidelines, which provide for refunds subject to the applicable timelines and permit a processing charge of no more than Rs 1,000 in the circumstances covered by the rules.It also noted that the institute had not produced evidence to justify retaining the balance amount. The complainant's evidence that the student had withdrawn before the academic session and had not availed of educational services remained unrebutted.“Accordingly, this Commission holds that the Opposite Party was deficient in service in refusing to refund the amount due to the Complainant. The act of retaining the entire amount by relying upon the printed non-refundable condition, in the circumstances of this case, also amounts to an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019,” it added.The commission said the complainant was entitled to a refund after the permissible processing deduction, along with reasonable compensation and litigation costs. However, it considered the demand for Rs 50,000 as compensation excessive.“The Complainant has claimed refund of Rs.29,500/- after deducting Rs.1,000/- towards processing charges. The said claim is reasonable in the facts of the case. The Complainant is also entitled to reasonable compensation for the inconvenience and harassment caused and to litigation costs,” the bench further added.Final orderPartly allowing the complaint, the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Ranga Reddy, directed IIHMCA to:Refund Rs 29,500 to the complainant after deducting Rs 1,000 towards processing charges.Pay Rs 5,000 as compensation.Pay Rs 5,000 towards litigation expenses.The total amount ordered to be paid to the complainant is Rs 39,500. The institute must comply within 45 days of receiving the order.The commission did not grant the 12 percent annual interest sought by the complainant.

articles.title: After testifying in sexual assault cases, Scottish survivors Sarah Lee, 39, and Kayla Poulton, 36, launched CourtRobe, a campaign seeking donated clothing and trained stylists for women appearing in court
articles.summary: Two sexual assault survivors in Scotland, Sarah Lee, 39, and Kayla Poulton, 36, have launched a campaign called CourtRobe to help women feel more
articles.body: Two sexual assault survivors in Scotland, Sarah Lee, 39, and Kayla Poulton, 36, have launched a campaign called CourtRobe to help women feel more confident when giving evidence in court. The initiative provides free clothing and personal shopping support, particularly to women on limited incomes.The two women are working with the Emma Ritch Law Clinic at the University of Glasgow and are seeking clothing donations and shopping vouchers from department stores across Scotland.According to a BBC Scotland report, participating shops would offer free personal shopping appointments, allowing women to choose outfits they feel comfortable wearing. Staff would also receive specialist training to understand the difficulties faced by sexual assault survivors.For Sarah and Kayla, the idea came from their own experiences of giving evidence. Both had been through the court process and remembered how much they worried about their appearance. They feared that the people listening to their evidence might form opinions about them based on their clothes rather than what they had to say.The two women now want to make that part of the experience easier for others. They believe that while CourtRobe cannot remove the pressure of giving evidence, having suitable clothes and someone to help choose them could reduce some of the anxiety women face before entering the courtroom.The beginning of CourtRobeSarah described her trial as one of the darkest periods of her life. Alongside the pressure of giving evidence, she found herself repeatedly questioning what she should wear and how she would be judged.She told BBC Scotland News that even small decisions about her appearance became a source of concern. She wondered whether her clothes should be more covered, how her hair would look and what impression she might make on others."There's just all these questions, how will my hair look? You're anticipating that people are going to put you on trial," she said.Kayla faced similar worries, although her concerns centred on particular clothing choices. She considered wearing a dress but feared it might be seen as too provocative. She also questioned whether heels would be suitable.Eventually, she chose suit trousers and a blouse. However, that did not put an end to her worries, as she then became concerned that the blouse might be see-through."You just overthink. You don't want people to think, oh, she deserved that. Oh, if she dressed like that, then, well, she deserved it," she said.Can clothing influence how witnesses are judged?The concerns raised by Sarah and Kayla are not limited to their personal experiences. As per the report, Rape Crisis Scotland pointed to research suggesting that a witness's appearance can influence how their evidence is received in sexual assault trials.Nicola Love, a spokeswoman for the organisation, said research involving juries had shown that witnesses could be considered less credible if their clothing was regarded as revealing or provocative.Love said it was therefore understandable that women might be especially worried about how they would be perceived while giving evidence.She also highlighted the financial difficulties associated with attending court, saying the costs involved were not discussed enough.You use AI every day. articles.title: Working one's way up
articles.summary: A man entered a certain recruiting office and said, “I want to join as a soldier.” “But how old are you?” the sergeant asked.
articles.body: A man entered a certain recruiting office and said, “I want to join as a soldier.”“But how old are you?” the sergeant asked.“Sixty,” was the man’s reply“You know quite well that sixty is too old for you to become a soldier.”“All right, if 60 is too old for a soldier, don’t you need any generals?”If one wants to start one’s career as a general, one will be hard put to it to do so. It’s just like a race where one can’t leap straight from the starting point to the finishing line. To succeed in anything, we have to be like the tree, starting from the seed, growing slowly and putting out branches, twigs, leaves and flowers when the appropriate times come around. Similarly, business starts with investing money, not with earning profits. The construction of a house starts with the laying of the foundation, not with the tiling of the roof. The factory begins with the acquisition of machinery and not with the sale of the end products. Congregational matters are very much on a parallel. They begin from the inculcation in individuals of a sense of purpose and an understanding of the importance of hard work, honesty, endurance and unity.Not until the individuals of a nation are imbued with these important ideals to a very high degree can measures be taken for the advancement of the cause. If we ignore the importance of preconditioning, our missionary ventures are bound to end in failure. Any attempt to launch a movement without a solid, national infrastructure would be like trying to roof a house without raising its walls. A roof put up in this way is bound eventually to collapse on one’s head. In much the same way, any steps taken before individuals have been properly prepared for them will lead inevitably to failure and chaos—even death and destruction. They will be found to lead only further and further away from the true objectives.Authored by: Maulana Wahiduddin Khan

articles.title: PhonePe launches Tatkal NPS, enables instant pension account opening with Rs 250 investment
articles.summary: PhonePe has launched ‘Tatkal NPS’ on its platform in partnership with leading banking institutions, allowing users to open a National Pension System (NPS)
articles.body: PhonePe has launched ‘Tatkal NPS’ on its platform in partnership with leading banking institutions, allowing users to open a National Pension System (NPS) account digitally and begin retirement planning with contributions starting at Rs 250. The digital payments and financial services company said the new offering is aimed at making long-term retirement planning more accessible to millions of Indians through a fully digital and paperless onboarding process. The service enables users to create a government-backed pension account and obtain a Permanent Retirement Account Number (PRAN) within minutes without the need for fresh document uploads or additional KYC procedures.According to PhonePe, the Tatkal NPS service allows customers to complete account opening in three simple steps by leveraging existing bank KYC records. The platform has integrated with leading banks to facilitate seamless onboarding, with plans to broaden coverage across the banking sector in the future. The initiative is powered by the Tatkal NPS framework developed by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA). Under this mechanism, users can authenticate themselves through a one-time password (OTP) linked to their bank account, enabling secure reuse of existing KYC details. This eliminates paperwork and significantly reduces the time required to open an NPS account.PhonePe said the offering is designed to appeal to a wide spectrum of users, including first-time financial planners, millennials and Gen-Z consumers. By lowering the minimum contribution amount to Rs 250, the company aims to encourage early retirement planning among younger Indians.The company also highlighted that the service could be particularly useful for gig workers, freelancers and small business owners who may not have access to employer-sponsored retirement benefits. The micro-investment approach is intended to make disciplined retirement savings more accessible to individuals across income segments.How users can open a Tatkal NPS account on PhonePeUsers can access the service by searching for “NPS” within the PhonePe app and selecting the National Pension Scheme option. They can then start the pension account journey, choose their linked bank account, authenticate it using a bank OTP, and make an initial contribution starting from Rs 250 through PhonePe UPI. Once the process is completed, a PRAN is generated instantly.With the launch of Tatkal NPS, PhonePe is expanding its financial services portfolio while seeking to drive greater participation in formal retirement savings among India's growing digital user base.You use AI every day. articles.title: A casual Instagram post, a swim in a hidden Colombian lagoon and a scientific mystery: How one giant waterlily turned out to be a new species unknown to science for millions of years
articles.summary: A casual Instagram post, a swim in a secluded Colombian lagoon and a team of scientists eventually revealed a remarkable botanical discovery.
articles.body: A casual Instagram post, a swim in a secluded Colombian lagoon and a team of scientists eventually revealed a remarkable botanical discovery. In 2021, plant enthusiast Jeremiah Harris photographed giant waterlilies in Colombia, assuming they belonged to a known species. Years later, those images helped scientists identify Victoria colombiana, a giant waterlily that had remained unknown to science despite potentially millions of years of separation from its relatives.When an Instagram photo raised an unexpected questionIn May 2021, Harris was exploring the flooded forests around Inírida, in Colombia's Guainía region, with local guides and fellow explorers. Their boat reached a hidden lagoon where enormous floating leaves covered the water.The plants looked like the familiar giant waterlily Victoria amazonica. Harris photographed them, took a swim among the lilies and shared the experience on Instagram.But the location raised a scientific question. No Victoria waterlily had previously been recorded from the Orinoco basin. Carlos Magdalena, a senior botanical horticulturist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, noticed the photographs and began investigating.A giant waterlily with clues of its ownThe team used satellite imagery to locate more populations. The leaves were large enough to be visible from space, making them easier to spot across the remote landscape.However, identifying a new plant species requires more than an unusual photograph. Scientists must compare physical features and examine how the plant differs from known relatives.The team eventually documented distinctive characteristics, including a cube-shaped ovary with sunken sides. Its prickles were also shorter, denser and softer than those of some related giant waterlilies.These differences helped establish that the plant was not simply another population of a familiar species.The race to find a flowering plantThe scientific investigation required fieldwork. Magdalena and his team travelled to Colombia to collect leaves and flowers, essential material for formally describing the species.Finding a flowering plant proved difficult. With their return flight to Bogotá approaching, the team faced the possibility of leaving without the samples they needed.Then, at around 11pm, boatman Gustavo Melo, from the Indigenous Tucano community, said he knew where more lilies could be found. The team travelled through the rainforest and reached a small lake shortly before sunrise.There, they found flowering plants and collected the necessary samples before returning for their flight.What makes Victoria colombiana special?The species are formally described in a 2026 paper published in Phytotaxa. Its floating leaves can reach 2.5 metres across, while its bright green leaves and softer prickles distinguish it from some relatives.Like other Victoria species, its flowers bloom over two nights, closing during the day between blooms.Its home also matters. The plant grows in the upper Orinoco drainage, a river system separated from the Amazon basin over geological time. The researchers suggest that changing river courses and long periods of isolation helped different Victoria species evolve.The study recognises five accepted species in the genus, including Victoria colombiana and Victoria mattogrossensis, identified in the Pantanal region.A discovery that raises conservation concernsThe discovery comes with a warning. Estimates suggest only around 30 to 50 individual Victoria colombiana plants remain in the wild, potentially placing the species in the critically endangered category.Researchers are working with Indigenous communities to collect seeds and study ways to grow the plant under controlled conditions. One proposed approach involves establishing a protected lake that could also support carefully managed ecotourism.The story also is a reminder about botanical exploration. Indigenous communities and local guides often hold detailed knowledge of landscapes that remain difficult for outside researchers to reach. Their contributions are essential to documenting and protecting rare plants.A photograph shared for its beauty ultimately helped reveal a species previously unknown to science. The lagoon had held its secret in plain sight, waiting for the right questions to be asked.Disclaimer: This article is based on the supplied research summary and study details.
